title: Clare's sisters
hook: enclosed, poor and joyful, praying for the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birds: Francis preaching to his little sisters, and the flock flying off in a cross. Your line was sisters birds. Did one sing long enough for you to stop? Day one thousand two hundred fifteen.

Night in Assisi. A young woman from a noble family slips out of her father's house, by a side door, tradition says, and hurries down the hill to the little church where Francis and his brothers live. They meet her with torches. There, in front of the altar, she lays aside her fine clothes, and Francis cuts off her hair. Her name is Clare. Soon after, at the convent where Francis has sent her, her family comes and tries to bring her home, and she holds on to the altar there and won't let go. She has seen the life Francis is living, and she wants it too. Today, the women who followed her, and the hidden life they chose.
screen: `A DOOR OPENS AT NIGHT.` → `TORCHES, AND HER HAIR CUT.` → `SHE WON'T GO HOME.`

segments.voice: Clare settles at San Damiano, the small church Francis had rebuilt with his own hands. Other women come to join her, her own sister among them, and they become the Poor Ladies, known today as the Poor Clares. Their life has three marks, and the first is poverty. Clare holds on to it fiercely. Her early biography says a pope once offered to free her from her vow of poverty, so the sisters could own property and be secure. She told him she never wanted to be freed from following Christ. What she asked for instead was a privilege: the right to own nothing at all. The second mark is enclosure. The sisters stay inside the monastery walls. Visitors speak to them through a grille, and the world mostly goes on without seeing them. To an outside eye that can look like hiding. Clare saw it as making room. Jesus says in the gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, "enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret." The enclosure is a whole life lived behind that shut door. And the third mark is the one an outsider might not expect: joy. Clare's letters to Agnes of Prague, a princess who chose the same life, are full of it. She tells Agnes to gaze into Christ as into a mirror, every day, and to see herself there. These are not letters from someone who feels trapped. And the prayer behind the walls isn't only for the sisters themselves. Poor Clares pray for the world outside, for the people who'll never know their names. Hidden, in their tradition, doesn't mean absent. It means close by, unseen, holding things up.
screen: `POVERTY: THE PRIVILEGE OF OWNING NOTHING.` · `ENCLOSURE: BEHIND THE SHUT DOOR.` · `JOY: CHRIST AS A MIRROR.` · `PRAYING FOR A WORLD THAT DOESN'T SEE.` · then, large: `PRAY TO THY FATHER IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the people who pray unseen. Settle, and breathe. Somewhere right now, behind a wall you'll never walk through, there are sisters at prayer. You don't know their names, and they don't know yours. Hold them in mind for a moment. Then widen it: the grandmother who prays every night for a family that doesn't ask her to, the friend who quietly keeps you in mind. If you pray, you can pray for the enclosed sisters, and for anyone who carries others in hidden prayer. If you don't, simply send them your thanks into the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Poor Clares. The sisters who follow Saint Clare: poor, enclosed, joyful, praying for a world that rarely sees them. Today's word.
Your line: hidden prayer. Today, do one good thing for someone, or hold them in mind, without telling them or anyone else. Day one thousand two hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Poor Clare monasteries live in enclosure and pray the Liturgy of the Hours through the day, and some Catholics send them prayer requests by letter or leave them at the monastery door.

fork.setup: you're Clare. a pope offers to free you from your vow of poverty, so your sisters can own property and be secure. what do you say?
options: accept a little land, but nothing more.
say you never want to be freed from following Christ.

original.note: Latin: enclosure, the closed life of a monastery.

trapdoor: what you thought: nuns who shut themselves away from the world.
what it means: sisters who stay behind the walls to pray for the world, poor and glad of it.
what a scholar hears: Clare fought for the privilege of poverty, and her letters to Agnes of Prague are a key source for her own voice.

notes: Clare's flight: the side door ('door of the dead') and Palm Sunday are tradition; kept as 'tradition says' and the date omitted. Check: met with torches at the Portiuncula; hair cut by Francis; clinging to the altar when her family came.
The pope's offer and Clare's reply are paraphrased from the Legend of Saint Clare (usually attributed to Thomas of Celano; refers to Gregory IX). Confirm; pope left unnamed.
Privilege of poverty: confirm framing as 'the right to own nothing'.
'Poor Ladies' as an early name: confirm.
Mirror image paraphrased from Clare's letters to Agnes of Prague (third and fourth letters); confirm.
howItsDone: prayer requests to Poor Clare monasteries; confirm 'often'.

Editor pass: the hook had Clare's family seizing her at the church where Francis lived; the Legend places the clinging-to-the-altar scene at the convent (San Paolo delle Abbadesse) where Francis sent her afterward, so the line now says so without naming it. howItsDone 'often' softened to 'some Catholics'.
